tierWindow.goal: Deliver a presentation well across the formats used for assessment: choose an approach that fits the brief, structure and design it to support delivery, and correct the errors that weaken it.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Application and analysis (adapt, structure, design, distinguish and correct), building on the introductory understanding of what a presentation is.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Realistic presentation tasks with several moving parts: a format, a brief, a structure, visual aids and a live delivery to manage together.
tierWindow.autonomy: Moderate scaffolding; worked examples model the moves, then the learner applies them; feedback explains the reasoning, not only the answer.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner already knows what a presentation is and how one is put together (the introductory course, or equivalent experience). They have given presentations but want them to land: this course is about delivering well across formats, not about defining the task from scratch. Group work and collaboration are held back for the advanced tier.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, choosing your approach for the format: reading the brief so your preparation fits. Second, structuring and designing for delivery: building a structure and visual aids that carry the audience. Third, avoiding common delivery errors: spotting and correcting what undoes a presentation. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about delivering a presentation well, across the formats you meet at university. You already know what a presentation is; here you build the skills that make one land. By the end you will be able to adapt your approach to a format and brief, structure and design a presentation that supports your delivery, and spot and correct the errors that weaken it.

Presentations are assessed in almost every subject, and the same skills carry into interviews and professional life. Delivering well is not about confidence alone. It rests on preparation that fits the task, a structure the audience can follow, and the judgement to avoid the common pitfalls.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: adapt your approach to the format and brief, structure and design for delivery, and identify and correct common errors.

practiceConnection.academic: Presentations run through your degree and beyond it. Every assessed talk, poster, group pitch and seminar presentation draws on the same skills: reading the task, building a structure, and delivering without the common errors. Build them now and they carry into interviews, meetings and the professional presentations your working life will ask of you.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced presenting course takes you into presenting with authority and collaborating, including group work, the roles people take, and handling disagreement. Going wider: the same skills support Academic Writing, where structure and argument matter, and Reflective Practice, where you review how a delivery went and improve it.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Delivering a presentation well is no longer a matter of nerve alone: it is a set of choices you can make on purpose. You can read a format and its brief and adapt your preparation to fit. You can build a structure, with an introduction, an ordered body and a clear conclusion, and design visual aids that support it. And you can spot the common errors that undo a presentation, and correct them before the day. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, delivering well is something you practise in every presentation you give. Each time you read a brief, build a structure, or cut a slide to a prompt, these skills are at work. They travel beyond your degree too: interviews, pitches and workplace briefings all reward the presenter who prepares for the task and avoids the common errors.

Which of these is a common presentation error rather than a sound delivery choice?
